cap: Type I endometrioid carcinoma follows a long estrogen-driven road: unopposed estrogen causes hyperplasia, cytologic atypia marks the step to endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, and PTEN loss and mismatch repair defects appear early, so tumors are usually low grade and found early through postmenopausal bleeding. Type II serous carcinoma arises in the atrophic endometrium of older women through an early TP53 mutation and is high grade from the start.
teach: Read the two roads as two different diseases. On the type I road, unopposed estrogen drives hyperplasia, atypia marks endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, and PTEN loss and mismatch repair defects appear early; because Lynch syndrome inherits the repair defect, an endometrioid cancer can be the first Lynch cancer. The tumor is low grade and indolent, and depth of myometrial invasion sets the stage. On the type II road, the atrophic endometrium of an older, thin woman acquires a TP53 mutation, an intraepithelial serous carcinoma forms, and cells spread early through the tubes and peritoneum. Carcinosarcoma, a biphasic tumor with carcinomatous and sarcomatous parts, behaves like this aggressive group.
